Good morning. How can I help?
I hope you can clear something up for me. I have been told three different things about the boat this morning.
Three? Go on. Who told you what?

The woman on the phone told me it left at nine, and she assured me the booking was confirmed. Then your website said ten thirty. And the driver told me this morning that the whole trip had been cancelled.
I am sorry. Nine is the old time, the website is right, and nothing has been cancelled. The driver was talking about the fishing trip, so it is a misunderstanding and not a change.
So, word for word: the boat leaves at ten thirty today and my booking stands. Is that right?
That is right. And I will put you through to the operator now, so that you hear it from them as well.
Thank you. Could you also send me that in writing, straight away? Then nobody has to remember who said what.

I train front-desk teams, and there is one sentence I ask every new person to learn in the first week. It is not an apology. It is a question: who told you that, and when? Because almost every angry conversation at a desk is not really about the problem. It is about two people holding two different versions of the same fact, and neither of them knowing where the other version came from. Now, the same thing works from your side of the desk, and travellers almost never use it. If you were told something, say who told you and say it in their words. The woman on the phone told me the tour left at nine. That single sentence does three things at once. It shows the person in front of you that you are not inventing it. It gives them somebody to check with. And, this is the important part, it is not an accusation, because you are quoting, not arguing. The version that goes wrong is the one that starts with you people. The version that works starts with somebody told me. And if you can add when, you have handed them the whole problem in one line, and they can fix it in about twenty seconds.

I run day trips out of Miami, and I want to explain why you get three different answers to the same question, because it is almost never anybody lying to you. Our morning boat moves from nine to ten thirty in October, when the season changes. The phone team gets the new time on the first of the month. The website gets it when somebody remembers to edit the page, which can be a week later. And the drivers hear it from us on the morning it changes, which is why a driver may still be telling people about last week. Three sources, three ages of the same fact. So here is what I would ask for if I were you, and it is three things. Ask for a name, so you know who said it. Ask for a time, not soon and not later, an actual number. And ask for one line of it in writing, by message or by email, because writing is the only version that does not change when the shift changes. Do that once, at the start, and you will not have to ask anybody again.
